After the Design Thinking lecture of Module 1, I decided to implement visualization technique  in my coaching sessions to make it more effective.
I used “cross-road” to put their various options before  taking a decision.
These tools were selected so that I could go back to these  visuals to arrive at a common meeting point.
In first case, I asked the 2 co- founders in a coaching session, to draw their business plan for a year.

In second case, I asked my coachee to visualize a meeting with his client – I asked him to  visualize the room, the chair, table, clothes, smell, temperature, etc during the meeting –  then visualize the discussion.

In third instance, there were 2 founders and were not clear of the direction to move the  company – they had to choose from designing new product feature, go for angel funding,  develop skills in team, or a mix of any two.
Using that picture, we discussed about the path to choose that would finally lead them to the  final destination.
I realized that visualization is a great tool to be used in coaching as coaching is also about  energizing your right brain.
be patient and empathetic, should be able to connect the dots, etc. just like it’s mentioned in  this course.
Also, I see visualization can be applied more broadly in any situation where I have to explain  my point of view or understand others viewpoint.

Needless to say, at the end of these sessions, the founders, in all 3 cases, were very  pleased with the outcome as they could visually recollect the discussion!!

My job is to create ideas to convince clients to use Renewable Energy Sources
My customers need to understand how a house plus energy works
how they can charge an electric car for free and how they can use free energy at home
I want to sell products through education
We have to find ways to convince them to sustainability
we want to present the process online to reduce costs and time.
Selection: I personally chose the visualization for this task
I believe that this is the most effective method in my industry
I want to visually show the problem using examples and comparisons
we want to create a set of questions and answers for our problem
The team must construct the responses as simply as possible.
because it is really a key part of the way we communicate, whether we are aware of it or not.
It allows us to think non-verbally
I also know that the most important thing is to visualize the idea first
because then you will be able to test the prototype in the wild.
Each of the subsequent prototypes should be built with the user in mind and answer a specific question.
Application: The first way to visualize sustainable development and the use of solar energy for free electricity and charging an electric car was the Power Point presentation
The method turned out to be effective, but only in a small group of participants.
It required a presentation with an employee of our company who, through this tool, discussed the problem and educated our clients.
Unfortunately, it did not involve our client enough and turned out to be boring.
The second way is to prepare a solar calculator on the website
This turned out to be an easy, quick and cheap way to reach the customer and get his attention.
An important element was to show the customer a common denominator for photovoltaic installations.
Insight: Our team has built a design of a typical residential building
which they have placed on our website.
In the upper corner, the team has placed a column in which the client himself provided the approximate size of the roof.
The next column showed the location of the roof in relation to the geographical sides of the world (north, south, east and west)
The third column contained the price of the electric bill that the customer pays every month.
Due to the simplicity of the tool, we did not want to have more data than the three we need to visualize the solution of our client's problem.
After entering the data, our client received graphically how to use energy.
How many kilometers will the electric car travel.
How much will its cost of electricity decrease.
How many trees will the customer save by using renewable energy sources.
Approach: I believe that i can use this tool globally, but i need to change our team's approach to generating customer attention.
It is worth introducing a short video with the next tool that describes the basic energy problems of the client and our planet.

PERSON.text: Design Thinking in Career Development and Counseling

DATE_TIME.text: Looking inside: self assessment, analysis, synthesis
Design Thinking in general with its procedures and instruments appears to be useful in dealing with career development issues.

‘What is’ or ‘looking inside’ phase should not be cut short or skipped – even if the client is itching to apply for a new job immediately. ‘If you don’t know where you are going, you might end up somewhere else’ (C. Stengel) – but if you don’t know where you are coming from, you might get stuck in the middle of nowhere again and again.

For instance, if you ask a candidate in a job interview to tell his or her story rather than to take you through the stages of a polished résumé, the person will most likely open up (and tell you much more than previously intended).
These tools should be complemented by qualitative instruments like storytelling (Patton & McMahon, 1999, p.236).
Others get carried away as soon as they are taken seriously and obtain ‘permission’ to talk about themselves.

EMAIL.text: With almost twenty years of experience in organizational and people development, I have never knowingly applied design thinking methodologies or tools in order to solve business problems or people issues.
What is? Looking inside: self assessment, analysis, synthesis

It may help finding answers to the question how to effectively design and propose a unique portfolio of competencies in a world of work that has become increasingly volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (Laurençon, 2014).

Narrative management encompasses personal and corporate storytelling, narrative knowledge management, leadership communications, and narrative change management (Erlach & Müller, 2015/2016). ‘Stories or narratives are a unique derivative of systems theory thinking and are key to constructivist approaches’ (Patton & McMahon, 1999, p.235).
We all have a personal story to tell with a myriad of twists and turns, touch and pain points.
3. Application There are basically two reactions: a smile or a blank face.
• Tell me be about your career to date.
• What career paths have you been following?
• What do all of your jobs/assignments have in common?
• What are the highlights of your job history or career chronology?
• What is your current level of satisfaction at work?
• How do you define success and how will you know it when you have it?
What is it for you to have a full, rich life?

The client will interpret his or her background and uncover the influence of significant others, i.e. the roles in the career story: protagonist and antagonist (a person or a barrier), objectives and helpers or mentors (Erlach & Müller, 2015, p.5).
This includes dealing with change, challenges, and conflict as the key to and starting-point of any story (Sammer, 2014, p.117; Patton & McMahon, 1999, p.177).
For example, one of my clients used to constantly point out negative issues of her career in an interview. As a consequence she gathered a depressingly high number of rejections to her applications.

It may sound contradictory, but knowing and understanding the value of storytelling as a powerful instrument of design thinking enables me to combine it more effectively with other selected and individualized tools (e.g., card sorts, work diaries) in career counseling sessions.
Thus, I initially need to find out what kind of career assessment method the person may prefer.
However, storytelling should always be the key instrument. It does not have to be called storytelling explicitly as this may put some people off.
With a few WHY questions he could not escape, we broke the ice and got to the core of his career issues.

PHONE.text: I was not even aware that design thinking exists. Thus, it struck me by surprise when I discovered the similarities between the design thinking approach (Malak, 2016) and the career coaching process based upon systems theory, success strategy and cybernetics (Friedrich, Seiwert and Geffroy, 2003, p.23):
What if? Looking outside: orientation, options, and evaluation  What wows? What works?  Looking forward: career action plan design and implementation

Challenge A typical challenge in career counseling is to help the client discover and understand his or her own work life story and its patterns without providing answers or even advice. Normally, people are not used to analyzing their own history and development including a reflection of their values, motivated skills, preferred work settings and satisfiers, barriers and constraints.

Selection In this initial stage of the career coaching process the instrument of choice is storytelling. Storytelling is not just a design thinking tool (Malak, 2016, Module 2) but also the foundation of narrative management and communications in a broad variety of contexts (Sammer, 2014, p.36).
Storytelling is very useful in human resources management in general, e.g. in recruitment and selection.
We all love stories. We love to use our episodic brain. We ‘think’ in stories and tend to forget unrelated facts (Erlach & Müller, 2015, pp.3-4; Sammer, 2014, p.1).

So, administering standardized and primarily quantitative assessment tools (e.g., surveys or psychological tests) in career counseling to gather data, analyze types, and pigeonhole someone is definitely not enough and does not do justice to a person’s individuality and character.
Consequently, I start the career counseling process with a seemingly simple question: What’s your story?
In our world of ‘hard facts’ many people have forgotten how to tell stories, especially their own.
In order to assist the client I ask guiding and probing questions (Guerriero & Allen, 1998, pp.26-37 and own compilation), for example:
• What were you trained for in school/college/university?
• What do you regret/resent?
• Which achievements are important to you and why?
• What have been the most rewarding/disappointing components of your jobs?
• Have you been repeating some of the same employment patterns that did not feel right for you?
• Have you ever thought that you would be happier in a different work environment?
• When you are ninety-five years old, what will you want to say about your life?

Telling one’s life and career story will assist the client with uncovering patterns and themes and forgotten events, making meaning of his or her own career, understanding experiences, and re-constructing (Patton & McMahon, 1999, p.148, p.177 and p.235).
S/he will be able to deal with (suppressed) emotions and focus on the WHY rather than the WHAT of his or her career development to date.

Eventually, the client will find his or her unique strengths, motivated skills, and a potential compelling offer (Friedrich, Seiwert and Geffroy, 2003, p.23) based upon what constitutes individual success and failure.
Once she was able to re-frame her own story, she came across much more self-confident and convincing and succeeded in obtaining a position in a suitable work environment.

Career counseling is like working on a puzzle with a dizzying number of pieces. With the help of storytelling the client will build and eventually see the bigger picture (Malak & Malak, 2011, pos.1028), i.e. his or her unique work life ‘paint’.
4. Approach As mentioned previously, I sometimes encounter clients whose approach to any kind of work issue is driven by facts and figures (e.g., the stereotypical engineer or financial analyst).

If s/he is more of a straightforward, analytic, numbers, procedures (you name it) type, other tools quickly providing structure (e.g., mind mapping, questionnaires, bullet point lists), may be more appropriate to begin with.
Apart from this, some may need more or different probing questions than others.

For example, one client told me right away that he was not interested in telling stories but in producing results fast and furiously. He was convinced that it was my job to provide the network, contacts, and leads he needed.

Ultimately, when applying storytelling in a career counseling session I need to avoid jumping to conclusions too fast or steering the client into a specific direction (in order to confirm my own ideas or assumptions).

PERSON.text: A boy named John was upset.
John did as he had been told.
In life, things happen around us, things happen to us, but the only thing that matters is how you choose to react to it and what you make out of it.

PHONE.text: He placed them in three bowls.
His father then boiled all three bowls.

DATE_TIME.text: When his father asked John why he was crying, he said that he had a lot of problems in his life.
He then asked John to feel their texture and then fill each bowl with water.
Once the bowls had cooled down, John’s father asked him to feel the texture of the different food items again.

John noticed that the potato had become soft and its skin was peeling off easily; the egg had become harder and tougher; the coffee beans had completely changed and filled the bowl of water with aroma and flavour.
Life will always have problems and pressures, like the boiling water in the story. It’s how you respond and react to these problems that counts the most!
Sometimes adversity is what you need to face in order to become successful.
Life is all about learning, adopting and converting all the struggles that we experience in to something positive.
Never give up. We should face every problem and find the solution for it.
Solving problems and not giving up gives us more confidence.

The main challenge is how to make work faster and avoid bulk transactions during month end to ensure better efficiency.

The tool that I selected for my challenge is learning launch. It is a tool that turn ideas into experiments in order to test a hypothesis. It is figuring out what the customers and the organization need. It is to get the truth and then the truth either confirms or dis-confirms your assumptions.

The tool gave us ideas on how to document and book at a faster pace such as creating a database specific to each branch or developer wherein it will serve as a tool for account updates, and shall also include security protocols in order to protect privacy of the bank and its customers.

DATE_TIME.text: It was hence essential to understand the target audience’s behaviour, not restricted to the sanitation habits, but also about the overall way of life.

ADDRESS.text: As part of my role as a Consultant to the Govt. on the ‘Sanitation for all’ project

PHONE.text: we faced a challenge where we found that the mere availability of the physical infrastructure, i.e. toilets, was not leading to higher usage of toilets for safer sanitation, by our target audience in rural areas.
Earlier solutions were neither human-centered (Week 1-Video 1 and Week 1-Video 5), nor based on customer empathy (Week 2-Video 3).
The task at hand required engaging with people and making them interested to collaborate and co-create a solution which is sustainable (Week 4-Video 5).

While we chose more than one tool since the task was multi-fold – to understand the behaviour (Journey Mapping, Week 1-Video 3), and then be able to involve and co-create a sustainable solution (Mind-Mapping, Week 3- Video 2; it was Storytelling as a tool (Week 2-Video 4), that i am explaining for this assignment.

Storytelling not only helps the audience build interest in, relate with and visualise the context, but also creates a space for feedback and comments, which was valuable in our case since sanitation is not a subject that people wanted to openly talk about anyway.

We wanted to make our storytelling exercise a coherent, relatable and interesting one, which will not only encourage the target group to get involved in it, but also have an emotional connection, which is critical.
The ill-effects of poor sanitation practice were conveyed in form of a story which had characters in it, who had a similar lifestyle as that of the target audience who was listening to story.
Essentially, this was a space that was left for others to contribute (Week 4-Video 7).

Since the solutions came from the target group themselves, there was a sense of ownership and co-creation in the target group that led to higher compliance and engagement with the solutions implemented on ground.

EMAIL.text: This was more of a behavioural issue than anything else.
The core challenge was to bring about a behavioural change in the target audience w.r.t. sanitation habits, which would lead to higher usage of toilets and adoption of safer sanitation practice.
Human beings love stories, and more so when stories are relatable to them, or about them.
Storytelling as Design Thinking tool was picked up to build a connection with our audience.
It was also the easiest medium to convey a message for the kind of target group that we wanted to address.
The stories were built around the specific community and village or hamlet, and characters were named same as some of the people there.
However, endings of the stories were not disclosed. This was to build suspense (Week 2-Video 4), and more importantly to keep space open for discussion and feedback.
We also left the story at a point that various solutions to tackle the challenge of behavioural change can come from audience themselves, hence increasing the participation from the group.

The tool was then implemented at multiple places with a bit of tweaking depending upon various extraneous factors, but led to a positive result in terms of engagement, collaboration, co-creation and sustenance of solutions.

DATE_TIME.text: Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

In my initial assessment of the problem, I identified two key issues: first, familiarity with Agile was not  consistent or uniform across the project teams, and in an engineering organization, that level of ambiguity  and open-ended planning creates more than a little bit of angst.
Application: Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., what you did and  how the tool was applied effectively or ineffectively).

The uncertainty that is inherent in the Agile methodology is not comfortable for aerospace engineers,  but walking them through the process of identifying the "known knowns" and the "known unknowns" in  terms of current and future application of the work helped to temper this.

As a result of this testing and observation, the project team realized the need to continue with the  baseline project as originally specified, but with a built-in flexibility to adapt and rapidly create  communities of practice where the type of interaction and knowledge sharing that would happen  anyway could be harvested and captured for the future as well.

Insight: Describe the insight you gained from applying the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., how  an insight affected your thinking about the challenge and about design thinking more broadly).
The most significant observation I've made  through these years of consulting and with this project in particular is that, with engineers, it is very difficult  to overcome the need for certainty.
Approach: Describe what you might do differently next time -- applying the same tool you selected or a  different one -- and the reason(s) why.

ADDRESS.text: The company I consult with has been trying to move toward the Agile methodology for project management,  initially through the software engineering group and slowly expanding to other parts of the business.

PHONE.text: The main challenge that I encountered as a change management consultant is that, where software developers  have used Agile for most of their career, most of the engineering disciplines favor the waterfall approach.
Second, the adopted methodology for  change management across the corporation is heavily anchored in waterfall processes, and is, all by itself,  very rigid and bureaucratic.

In selecting the Learning Launch approach, I had to think of a quote from Donald Rumsfeld, former Secretary  of Defense, “… there are known knowns; there are things we know we know. We also know there are  known unknowns; that is to say we know there are some things we do not know.

By guiding the project team  through the discussion and answering the questions: "What do we know? What do we not know? What  do we need to know? How do we learn what we need to know?" I was able to get them to actively  reshape the project approach, and embrace the idea that what we were really working on was a product  that has customers internal to the organization, not a project that would be launched and checked off of  a list.

It also forced  the project team to realize that there was much that was unknowable as an entire body of knowledge  was being created in real time. To see how this would inform our approach to the project, we launched  a pilot initiative specifically focused on COVID-19 response, and observed the level of interaction,  engagement and contribution to the knowledge base that was possible without any direction.
And the project team acknowledged  that it was essential to adopt an Agile mindset to allow the product to evolve with the needs of the  business.
I have worked in organizational development and change management for over a decade, and most of that  time has been spent with engineers and software developers.

Acknowledging the inherent tension between the known and the unknown, and helping the project team see this as a call to action to think differently about scoping the  project and testing different approaches, made it possible to guide the shift to a new mindset and an  iterative approach to the project.

By proving that the modified version of our project and change model was able to flex to the immediate and  unanticipated needs of the business, and in the process to become an incredibly valuable resource to the  organization, we were able to reach a level of comfort with the unknown, allowing for the possibility of co-creation of solutions based on the real-time needs of our internal customers.

EMAIL.text: As  a result, project teams struggle with the notion of iterations and sprints when they are used to having the  entire project plan in place before starting.

We knew why we had been tasked to create the in-house capability to support knowledge management  and to facilitate access to a repository of data. What we could not have anticipated, but where we  suddenly had a use case to test from start to finish, was how COVID-19 and the need for information  about its effect on our business would drive adoption of the capability we were building.

To bridge the knowledge gap and begin moving in the direction of a more Agile approach, I selected the Learning Launch tool as a way to test some assumptions and possible approaches without creating unwarranted disruption with the ongoing project efforts.

COMPANY.text: that’s me and a fellow student
worked on a business idea within the sustainability realm
We thought of offering an easy way to compensate greenhouse gases to everyday people by becoming a
In other words, people would signup to a monthly subscription and the thereby provided money would be used to acquire land in their local area
1. acquire land in their local area
2. plant trees on that land and nurture those trees.
The offer would have been easily accessible through the web and mobile phones.
Our main challenge was to find out whether the business model would be sustainable / profitable at some point in the future
In other words, we needed to know whether people are interested in buying such subscriptions at all and if they were, how much they were willing to pay.
Of course, we could have gone out and simply survey potential customers w.r.t the two main questions mentioned above
But as people often tend to say one thing and ultimately do the other thing
we weren’t happy with this approach
We wanted to go with an approach that simulates the actual customer experience and therefore the actual customer behavior as closely as possible
And, as we wanted to keep the costs as minimal as possible – after all we still were students
As this matched many of the criteria described by Jens Hoffmann in the lecture “Tool: Learning Launch” of week 4
we decided to perform a Learning Launch
In other words, we went on to define our core hypotheses
2. setup a cheap and fast experiment generating the data needed to evaluate those hypotheses
4. evaluate the gathered data against our hypotheses.
We continued by setting up a landing page
This landing page was as close to the real website as it could be
On this website we explained what we are trying to do, why this is a good thing and why one should buy our product
Those explanations were followed by the actual product offerings
We provided multiple, exceedingly bigger offers at different prices
The only difference to a real offer was that at this point one could not buy those offers
Instead, each offer provided an individual button to subscribe to our notification service
This notification service would inform users once the actual offer was available
Experiment 1: Are people interested in this product?
Before launching the website, we clearly stated our disconfirming facts as explained by Professor Ed Hesse in “Learning Launch Tool” in week 4 of this course
Basically, this hypothesis sounded like this:
Less than x% of visitors of our website are interested in the product and therefore sign up for any notification service.
Experiment 2: How much are people willing to pay for this product?
To answer the second main question explained above, people were able to subscribe to notifications at any price point thereby providing a first signal about how much they are willing to pay.
the hypothesis we wanted to disprove for each offer X at price P this:
Less than x% of visitors of our website sign up for the offer X at price P.
For each hypothesis, we defined a certain threshold for the conversion rate we needed to achieve to disprove the hypothesis
Those thresholds were derived from our calculations on when the business model would be sustainable.
After setting up the experiment, we launched the landing page, started a small marketing campaign to get traffic on the landing page and gathered the resulting data
We also chose a designated sceptic to avoid confirmation bias as recommended in the lecture already mentioned above

The challenge was levied upon my team from an executive management council, who knew we were a group that was very connected with the product, but also had a good deal of understanding of the problem, given that many team members were millennials.

For instance, we decided not to do a video focused on the technology behind our solution but on the impact it has on patients that went to a hospital to have an x-ray or other medical imaging study

A communication plan started 30 days in advance to notify the employees of the application pilot and invited them to try the test application

ADDRESS.text: I have a customer in the consumer goods industry

PHONE.text: they explored an opportunity to leverage mobile app technology
and simple applications were preferred over applications with too many layers
My team selected a Learning Launch which is a small experimental test to determine if the idea was viable in the marketplace or an internal user base
What my customer assumed to be true was that the workforce would be interested in receiving work related content quickly and conveniently through their personal mobile devices

Similar to the trade show Learning Launch for IBM, our team gathered information on additional key factors that would inform the application content, preferred deployment process and understand any risk or challenges that had not been discovered to date during the project
The application would be deployed in the first two weeks of the learning launch using a mix of trained contract employees and app team members
The team equipped with launch materials set up tables at multiple "high traffic" locations in the plant for visibility
Observations were collected after each of the three shifts for a brief discussion the next morning
Pivots in deployment processes or explanations of how the application would be used were done regularly throughout the first two weeks
For instance, the use of company Wi-Fi was not in scope but the use of personal data became a concern to many pilot users

After a review with leadership, company Wi-Fi access was opened up to the pilot users which drove more adopters, but started the discussion on new governance usage policies, and the need to review possible expansion of the Wi-Fi system to include new wireless access points to improve coverage
A technical concern that became a barrier to adoption was the employees' concern over "Big Brother" on their personal devices
Several questions arose over the concern of tracking and use of location services at the plant and home which were not part of the application but required explanation
All of these concerns would have to be addressed prior to a roll out to the entire manufacturing team nationwide

PHONE.text: Challenge
The current Task Management teams were  underutilized.

These Task Management teams saw  themselves as paper-pushers, and it was our job to help them reevaluate their  responsibilities, purpose, and their overarching mission to help them go from reactive  analysts to proactive strategists.
We began with our research phase, digging up old Task Management policies,  guidance documents, and even interviewing current and past Task Management  personnel.
Then we held numerous facilitated discussions where we put all current  Task Management personnel (stakeholders) in one conference room to learn about their  basic job tasks and prioritization.

After many meetings with no resolution or consensus  amongst the different teams, we decided that in order to branch out of the current “What  Is” or as we often heard in these sessions as “the way we’ve always done it” – to a new  realm of “What If” we would need to conduct a mind mapping exercise.
The stakeholders’ experience ranged  from approximately five years in their current task management role to merely three  months.
We pulled the research from our initial steps and asked all members to read the longer  documents prior to arrival.
We clarified that the intent of this session was to determine  all job competencies and responsibilities to then reach an ultimate job description or  ‘motto’ that everyone would agree on.
When participants arrived, we provided sticky  notes and markers to each stakeholder to jot down all ideas on the sticky notes, one  idea per note.
Then, the facilitator clustered the sticky notes on the white board based  on similarity.
We left the session with a handful of competencies that the  group agreed upon and we felt confident about the progression of our project.
Our mind mapping exercise was a very telling activity.
Notably, we learned that even  amongst teams of the same level in the organization, there were great differences in  expectations, responsibilities, and even employee morale.
We learned that there were  already some teams who held a mindset of being strategic influencers, and we then  leveraged their support throughout the project.
The mind mapping exercise provided us  with common job competencies and an overarching job description.
As we entered the  “What If” phase we were armed and ready to begin brainstorming the new job  responsibilities.
Admittedly, this project was conducted prior to learning this Design Thinking  methodology and exercises.
In hindsight, this mind mapping exercise would have been  stronger if a wider net of stakeholders was cast.

If we had incorporated some of the leadership of the organization  in this exercise alongside the Task Management team members, there likely would  have been greater buy-in and a wider range of “What If’ statements in the brainstorming  phase.
We viewed mind mapping as a last resort when it should have been included in our  project plan all along.

PHONE.text: I have decided to take on the challenge and the opportunity to reinvent myself as an entrepreneur.
I offered to help and we got started on our early stage startup (code name: “The Box”)
so we needed to create common ground so we could communicate effectively and efficiently in order to build trust and commitment to our newly found mission together.

However, the Visualization tool for Design Thinking is quite different as it consists of using visual artifacts to express concepts, ideas and relationships in order to bring them forward in a way that words cannot.
We soon figured out that by making sketches and drawings we could reach mutual understanding much faster whenever we got stuck.

We started working on “The Box” as an ecommerce marketplace for subscription-based shopping, as we both knew many young entrepreneurs who are having trouble retaining their current customers and thought it would be a solution to their problem.

Once we had a better grip of the pain points and jobs to be done that our customers are facing, we used drawings to generate ideas of services, marketplaces and platforms that could help solve the problem.
We also got a bit ahead of ourselves and went ahead and drew lots of flywheels and virtuous cycles to represent potential growth models we should consider in order to accelerate growth.
I learned that in many cases verbal communication falls short when one is trying to simplify a concept that is complex or based on intricate relationships between basic ideas.

A key factor that makes visualization so helpful is that it makes metaphors like the “flywheel,” “cycles” and “platforms” easier to process intellectually because the relationship is evident at a glance.
Additionally, sharing drawings and sketches helps to build teamwork as it allows one to peek into each other’s mind.

EMAIL.text: Luckily, a few weeks after I left my previous job I met a college professor who was looking to build a startup but had not had the time to develop it into a working business.
Previously, I understood visualization as a creative exercise that consists of creating a realistic mental image of the future one desires in order to facilitate its realization.
My cofounder and I quickly learned that we were having trouble understanding each other because we would use terms that mean different things depending on the context.
Thus, we intuitively adopted the Visualization tool and made good use of it for our purposes.

We drew up many boxes and circles to represent all of the kinds of sellers we were thinking about, and by collecting them into a Venn Diagram we were able to make a preliminary segmentation in order to pick customers for ethnographic interviews:

At the moment, we are in conversations with a UX designer to build a working model of our service (not yet a prototype), based on these hand-drawn figures that describe the high-level steps for sellers and buyers:
Visualization is our favorite innovation tool!
On the other hand, using simple visualizations can help to transmit and receive messages in a more direct and clear way, even if the drawings are of very low quality from an aesthetic sense.
This may sound trivial but in the high-speed high-pressure world of startups it creates great efficiency and focus.
It is fun to use it that way.

PERSON.text: Challenge: Usually, I teach multicultural literature and creative writing. But this year, the director of my school asked that I teach U.S. History Because my understanding of U.S. History is shaped not by its most often taught historical events but largely by the writing and art created by marginalized peoples, I was not sure I had the knowledge of the traditionally rendered U.S. History curriculum and thus the skill-set to be successful. However, thinking of what I’ve learned about “growth mindset”, I accepted the challenge and reflected on the advantages I had in teaching this course: the most significant of which was that I had the benefit of having taught the students the previous year. Thus, I had a critical understanding of who the fifty-four students were and the challenges each faced in and out of the classroom. I also had the benefit of teaching at a progressive school that celebrates teacher creativity and divergent thinking.

Insight: Employing mind mapping in a classroom afforded me a few distinct privileges. The first is that it energized students and gave them a clear purpose that emphasized and celebrated their perspective and manner in which their thoughts diverge and converge. Students were liberated from any of the baggage related to writing, lack of self-confidence, challenges as English Language Learners, the tedious and arbitrary nature of grammar rules, the redundancy that began in first grade when writing is the measurement of creative and critical thinking capacity, and the static and sterile nature of a cursor blinking on the white page on a computer screen to name a few.

Approach: If I were to begin a course on learning about the experience of Native Americans in the United States again, I would begin the course with a mind mapping exercise on the first day, and then end the course with a final mind map. This would afford the students and I the opportunity to see and reflect upon the growth of our learning, and its trajectory and associations.

DATE_TIME.text: as part of a course of Problem-Solving Methodologies that we take in college
we were required to develop a project aimed at solving a soft problem in any kind of business or company
A soft problem is not related to problems like productivity of a manufacturing process o reducing costs from certain department
but it is a problem that aims to solve issues related to interpersonal relations among workers, or even with customers
we found a local clinical analysis laboratory that let us help them to deal with the increasing customer complaints that they were receiving
so the laboratory’s director told us to aim our project in improving the experience of the customer through the process that they have to go through to receive their service
When started analyzing the information that the laboratory gave us about their processes, how they measured satisfaction and even how the organization was structured
we realized that we had a lot of information to analyze and many stakeholders whose opinion was important and had to be taken into account
such as the customers, the customer service department, the chemical analysis department, and also the middle and top management
So, to understand their perspective of the problem, we interviewed many people from all the different areas involved
and after we gathered all the information about the interests and concerns of each of the stakeholders
we developed a visual representation of the process using a tool called Rich Picture, which is basically using drawings to graphically identify how a process flow

First, we drew the first sketch of the rich picture to have a better perspective of the information that we got from the historical data and the interviews to understand how the departments were interconnected
Them we had a meeting with the stakeholders to show them the sketch and explain the main issues that we found in it
so that they could give us some feedback about it, to effectively correct mistakes and create a final sketch that we could use to identify opportunities in the process

I think that applying this tool was great to start the project and for the stakeholders, because in a visual way we communicated our perspective of the process more effectively than just giving them an oral explanation of our findings
and that inspired them to give ideas of how the process could be improved to increase the customer satisfaction with the process

Applying this visualization tool (rich picture), we were able to have a broader perspective of the problem and suddenly the scope of the project increased because many other problems arose that were not directly related with how the customer was treated during the process
but also on how the information flowed across the different departments, having a lot of delays that caused a large lead time for the results to be sent to the customer
which at the end caused customer’s dissatisfaction
Also, as the drawings also facilitated the stakeholders understanding of the problem
the meeting was so productive because it became a brainstorming session in which they provided very useful ideas and potential solutions to the problem
and we were able to use that information for further analysis, using other useful tools, such as affinity diagrams and prioritization matrix
In my opinion, applying visualization tools is very useful for mapping processes and to identify opportunities to improve
and as we perceived during the project, it helped other people to understand our perspective of the situation and inspired them to share their thoughts
But, if I had an opportunity in the future to do a project with similar characteristics, I would use the journey mapping tool to follow the process from the client’s perspective

This is just what mind mapping does well.

Following the completion of extensive health-care industry research and in-depth interviews with members of the board to collect data on the current reality in the What Is? stage of the design thinking approach, we started the mind mapping process.

We began by asking the group to individually generate a set of planning assumptions about the likely future conditions that will impact the foundation and its work to help determine where members are aligned in beliefs about the future.
The group first noted these planning assumptions individually on Post-it Notes and pinned them on a large white board.
After all the ideas were exhausted following several rounds of the question “what else?”,

the team grouped the Post-It Noted ideas in the following themes: paying for health-care, “change” as a field, societal tone, politics, technology, process, and doing the work vs. paying for the work.
From this “map” of initial contributions, we asked the group to create an aligned-upon set of shared assumptions about the future context that the foundation will be acting in, starting in 2021.
In the next step, the board revisited the What Is?
stage research and brainstormed what they have found works to catalyze transformational systemic change, and what the field is saying about what the foundation might or should try.
Such ideas included creating new lines of business, partnering differently with localities, etc. These ideas were written on Post-it Notes and arranged on the white board.

The board then started anticipating potential future paths for the foundation by exploring two extremes: (1) be entirely organized as a think tank or (2) be completely focused on implementing current knowledge and practices.
The group split in two to explore these two possible approaches in depth.

The two teams suggested four alternate organizational realities to explore based on this experience: an implementation organization with some R&D (called “Alice”); a think tank with some implementation power (following the Alice in Wonderland theme, called “Mad Hatter”); taking on a program-based initiative to scale (“Cheshire Cat”), and having a “Mad Hatter”-like model that targets groups of leaders across systems instead of leaders of institutions alone (“Mock Turtle”).

Finally, the team closed out the mind mapping process by creating a summary chart to compare and contrast the four options to display how well each model could fulfill the foundation’s mission to further the state of health-care in the United States.

ADDRESS.text: My consulting firm was tasked by our client, a health-care foundation board, to help them design an organizational strategy in light of all the rapidly moving developments in health-care.

EMAIL.text: The board was at an impasse, uncertain on where to place their bets to best support health-care in this country without being able to predict where a number of current trends might lead.

COMPANY.text: We used design thinking to present a few high-level, flexible, iterative, strategic options for the board that the foundation could pursue within the 2021-2024 time-frame.

This reflection will focus on the mind mapping tool, which was the most important phase of the project as it moved the process from the What Is? stage of ascertaining the current state of the organization and of health-care in the U.S., to the crucial What If? stage of beginning to draft new, possible realities for the foundation.

I am defining mind mapping as the collective visualization by the board members of the sum of their knowledge, experiences, insights, interests, and visions of health-care, thereby establishing a snapshot or base upon which to build a series of possible strategic options for the foundation to pursue.

Design Thinking: Final Assignment Rhiannon Karim
I have recently completed a move, and the week-long process still haunts me.
After completing the modules of this course, it became apparent to me that design thinking can be applied to all aspects of my life.
My first chance to apply my knowledge occurred during my move. Let me take you back to three years ago, when I was purchasing my stereo system.
I had met a young salesman; whose passion was sound systems. I believe he has four personally built systems in his home to date.
After two hours, I left the store with a completely personalized package, a small map of connections he drew up for me, and an increasing sense of dread growing in my stomach.
Fast forward five hours. I am sitting on the floor in front of my television completely distraught and defeated: I could not get my system to work.
During my present day move, I was determined to complete the re-installation of my system independently.
I wish I could say I had the foresight to create my own mind map of the connections I had made, but who thinks of that before learning about Design Thinking?
My boyfriend connected the wires to my speakers, turned on the receiver, double checked the cables, and waited for sound.
None came. As he headed back to work from lunch, I set to work on conquering my system.
I did not want to experience the failure I did three years ago, and I was determined to be successful.
Before immediately jumping to frustration, I decided to try the design thinking approach because I needed a creative, systematic approach to a challenging problem that I was facing.
After I decided to try applying the tools of design thinking to this problem, I had to choose where I would start.
Clearly you start at the beginning, but that goes without saying. I decided to start my process with the visualization tool.
Being able to see the problem would allow me to explore the solutions.

The visualization tool forced me to think differently, as I was using the right side of my brain (instead of the left). Not only was it important that I define my problem, but it was also important that, as I moved through the design thinking process, I continued to utilize the visualization tool.
The visualization tool can be applied to the other design tools discussed in this course, thus carrying me throughout the entire process.

Visualization also allows the problem-solver to think in a nonverbal way. Too often I think in a linear, verbal manner; however, by using visualization, I could think in a more global, creative manner.
I selected visualization because it suggests I make a map or draw a picture of my problem.
I wanted to be able to utilize this map in the future if I needed it, so I felt like I was killing two birds with one stone.
The visualization tool suggested that I move through stages of exploration, pattern finding, ideation, prototyping, and scaling.

Step 1 - To start the process, I reviewed the existing business process flow documents and operational  training materials.

We created groups of location  heads responsible for dispatch system and accounts receivable personal and asked to identify the  activities involved in AR process.

Step 2 – Establishing effective billing and cash application to invoices process was one of the activity  identified by group, we decided to focus on it.
Using the visualization tool, we started drawing the  complete process.
The process involved origination of service order, order dispatching, invoice  generation, payment collection and applying to invoices.
The organization used the Ride Dispatch System  at each location for providing the on-demand service and generated the customer invoices.
The payments  were also collected at location.
The invoice and payment collection details are communicated by location  heads to central AR department and manually entered in ERP system.
The visual representation used  simple graphic to draw the picture of how the information flow from one system to another.
Insight -    Using the visualization tool, the stakeholders got the understanding of complete business  process flow which was not very transparent earlier.
The graphic also helped to gain the insight of  relationship between different systems across organization and how the information is tightly integrated  with each other.
It helped to work collaboratively to identify the improvement areas in business process.
The team got an insight of how the manual process created from two system created inconsistent report.
Using the feedback, the team developed a revised activity plan and decided to automate the invoice and payment information from dispatch system to ERP system.

PHONE.text: A friend of mine who is a businessman asked me for help to start the process of creating a business idea:
When they finished, I asked them to explain their drawing to me.
During the dialogue there were some new aspects that they remembered and had not included.

I wrote down all the explanations on my computer while they told me their experiences and went deeper with questions like: What exactly did you like about the massage? And did some indirect questions to know if they value the technology used in the centers like: What do you think of the equipment they use?
Did it help you?
All of the participants mentioned that the aspect they value the most is the quality of the massage, not depending on the technological devices, but on the therapist’s skills and profile.
They want a therapist who is: kind, skillfull, experienced,
quiet (that means he/she is not in a hurry to finish and transmits a peacefull feeling) and has an enterprise culture.
They said that in some cases, a less experienced therapist gave them a massage and it was obvious that he/she had more to learn.
One of the participants told me that once an intern gave her a massage and told her that she had an irreversible disease (which wasn’t true) and she got worried.
So in this first finding, my friend’s hypotesis doesn’t match the needs.
However there were other points to observe.
Every center has a main doctor who is the expert and the rest of the staff seems less experienced.
The participants value a lot when the main doctor treats them, because he/she gives them a better massage and a detailed explanation of their case.
This highlights another need to be covered: information.

Besides the doctor’s explanation, they didn’t mention elements that provide information about health problems, their health status (none of them have patients health histories) and most of them complained about not having a modern system that helps them to book an appointment (in two centers they can’t even call, the booking has to be on-site).
This is an opportunity for my friend to use technology to stand out from the competition.
The third most important aspect is the environment.

All of them mentioned that all of the centers had a bit dirty environments, with old furniture, some of them had old exercise machines, not so comfortable stretchers and the centers were located in non-commercial areas, but in households adapted to give the service.
One of the participants said that he liked a place where many patients had to sit around the same table while they got therapy through electricity.

This was nice because the equipment was new to him (he had received electricity therapy with other equipment before) and also because he got to know other people, share problems, solutions and socialize.
This goes combined with the need for information.
And finally, it is very important for them that the center is located not so far from their homes.
Two of them had to travel by bus one hour to get to the physiotherapy centers and in terms of cost/benefit they ended losing a lot of time and energy.
My friend told me he had ideas to bring the service to peoples homes, and to give them online service.

PERSON.text: Reflection: Mobile Money for the Unbanked-Storytelling
The person who helps one of my partners cleaning his house has shared with us the long and  complicated process that her mom faces triyng to receive these socials programs.
  The HardFact of the story is based on the challenges of the protagonist of the story and  not just in fixed data provides by reports/ market research.
She is Maria, a housewife with two small children who lives in the town of Zilacayotl, Municipality  of Acatepec, Guerrero, Mexico.
Maria receives social programs support from the government, such as food and money ....  However, making use of them is not an easy task.
Maria leaves  her house in the morning, motivated by not losing the bus and arriving as soon as  possible to Apetzuca, to neglect minimum her childrens and her home.
After arriving in Apetzuca and standing waiting for 2 hours under the sun's rays, Maria achieves to  receive the food and economic support from the government, now she can take the bus back  home.
However Maria knows that she still has the risk of being assaulted in the truck as it  happened last time.
Maria arrives at her home in the afternoon, fortunately there wasn’t any assault or accident in her  way.
His childrens are crying and ask her for food, because they haven’t eaten anything.
Maria is tired but she put the fire to cook something of the new food aid that was given to him and later she is  going to wash and to iron all the clothes that have pending as part of its work.
Is  fair that receiving help implies neglecting your home, children and other activities?
Just like the case of Maria, only 57% of the municipalities in Mexico have access to financial  services ... what about the other 43%?
Let's go back to Maria, every month her husband sends remittances to her and her children.
María againg has to travel form Apetzuca to other more far way place: the municipality of Tlatlahuque,  Guerrero which is 1 hour and 45 minutes from Acatepec.

DATE_TIME.text: She has to leave her childrens alone all day to move to Apetzuca, she has to leave very early from  her home because the bus that goes there leaves at 7AM and each new bus takes two hours to  pass again.

ADDRESS.text: I’m working on a project that increases economic development in rural areas with little or null  access to banking services.
Zilacayotl is a town far away from the big cities, where there is not internet, there is not 4G data,  not many institutions or banking services.
Apetzuca, a town that is 4 hours from her house, is the closest town where social programs are  distributed.
Tlatlahuaque is the nearest municipality  where you can find a bank and take remittances.

COMPANY.text: The current solutions focus only on two things: the funds to be  intended to social programs and the way they are delivered.
Well, they define the problem in a context that eliminates the opportunities  for innovation.

They attack the problem in a general way, assuming total certainty and prediction  based on statistical data without exploring the details and characteristics of the persons In these  communities, for example, giving money cards in areas where there is not access to services  where they can be used,

With the history  of her mom plus histories shared by other persons that have knowledge of this situation we have  design a solution to develop an economic growth, and bring closer financial services into these  zones.
Application    The first time we presented the solution we were focusing presenting the problem, the proposed  solution and the impact of this in the lives of these people.

Altought we did’t communicate a story,  we empathically connected the board members with the problem using an ethnographic  categorization and theorizing the results based on a similar solution applied in Africa where is a  success.
On the other hand, during the last presentation that we had with executives of another company  the results were different. We repeated the same formula that had previously given us success,
When we explained the scheme operation, they argued the use of electronic wallets that requires  a card to operate as a better solution.
The presentation has turned into a debate looking for  defend their ideas rather than a business/solution presentation.

We tried to make them see the problem with a focus on the needs of the person and problems of  infrastructure and lack of banking services that they experienced in their communities, to which  they argued with statistical and market data,
After all this, we have seen the need to create a story that communicates emphatic the situation  of the people and the problems they face.
We have tried to build a StoryTelling based on the following points:
  Using statistical information+results information from our investigation of the problem  (interviews, visualizing the problem) and then connect them with with the protagonist.
  Explain the current situation / problem based in  the emotional connection (empathy)
  Create moments of reflection through questions and suspense between them.
  The stresses that ignore the problem implies for the company.
  Communicate the strategy involved in the situation.
The bus cost is not cheap, the round trip is almost the same what she spend on the full food of one  day.
How is possible that we still allow localities and people staying disconnected from the world today,  being leaders in networks and connectivity?
Are they forgotten places where more families, including  men and women, face the same challenges as Maria?
The same story is repeated, alone childrens at  home, risk of assault on bus, long journey times and this time high commissions charged by the  bank,
Simply the payment of $ 20 trillion USD in remittance commissions and $ 10.6 trillion in G2P  transaction commissions (Goverment to person) and P2P (Person to person)
Again, why can’t we connect this forgotten sector to banking services?
Is the little social valuation that we give to these types of places and people or is the inexistence of  a business model that suits this type of scheme?

COMPANY.text: The organization that I work for specializes in "Loyalty" programs, which in my country is a  sector that has evolved very quickly, and over the 2 years since the launch, very good results  have been achieved and an important recognition in the market.

DATE_TIME.text: The challenge is to implement a new channel of interaction that allows for more fluid  communication with customers, which positively impacts their experience in each contact.

PHONE.text: The communication channel to be implemented is WhatsApp Business as a formal  communication channel, but the challenge is to clearly define what the scope of this new  channel will be according to the processes in the life cycle of the program and the requests  made by customers (Enrollment, Claims, frequently asked questions, user account  management) with the aim that this new channel may have a defined and specialized scope  focused on what customers in a channel like WhatsApp really value most.

FINANCIAL.text: When we were analyzing the different tools of design thinking, we identified that due to  the progress that has already been made in the different stages and the knowledge that we  have of our customers in the attention provided by the other channels of customer service,  the Learning Launch is the tool indicated in this stage of the project with which we will  quickly and economically test the hypotheses that we have raised and thus define the  appropriate scope for the new WhatsApp channel.

CREDENTIAL.text: Our Learning Launch process was considered in 2 stages: in the first stage, a list of  transactions that could be attended by the WhatsApp Channel was defined in order to  evaluate them in the Learning Launch and identify if the transactions that we consider in  our hypotheses that would be the most appropriate for this new channel, if indeed they  were those that the clients were requesting from us.

ADDRESS.text: For this test we defined that all the internal employees of the company will participate during a period of 15 days in order to  have fast, economic and close results with a critical public.

VEHICLE.text: We established an internal communication channel so that they could send us all the feedback and opportunities for  improvement and in this way make the necessary adjustments.

NETWORK.text: The experience in the application of the Learning Launch tool was very useful because it  allowed us to experiment and contrast the hypotheses we had about the scope that the  WhatsApp channel should have.

BIOMETRIC.text: Before the first stage, we were considering including the  option of “Enrollment” to the program through the new channel, since it is one of the  transactions that has the most impact on our telephone channel.

URL.text: But after the tests were completed, we were able to understand that as the “Enrollment” process is an activity that  requires significant time to complete and because it has other channels enabled, such as  the website, for this transaction in particular we were able to identify that customers  preferred to register by the other established channels, while the whatsapp channel gave  more relevance to interactions related to the FAQ´S, program information, password  change and failure reports.

ID.text: According to the above, the scope was redefined and additional  predetermined messages were adjusted, improving the customer experience in the new  channel much more.

EMAIL.text: MIND MAPPING
Feedback given to us facilitators was positive whereby participants did not feel fatigued as they could take their time to pen down ideas.

PHONE.text: CHALLENGE
This workshop managed to gather close to 70 unique user stories and these were all big ideas that had not been filtered to see ‘What Works’ because our CIO wanted us to think big!
Miro’s interactivity of the canvas whereby we could all see every participants cursor on the browser helped with keeping energy levels high as it was a fun and de-stressing activity for all.

ADDRESS.text: I was asked to co-facilitate a design thinking workshop within the Digital & Technology Sector of our organisation a few months ago, during the second wave of the pandemic in my country.

DATE_TIME.text: Our organisation recommended all staff to work remotely, thus our workshop had to adapt to a virtual environment which was new to not only the facilitators but participants.
At the end of the workshop, us facilitators recapped and debriefed each user story to all participants.

COMPANY.text: The intention of the design thinking workshop was to solicit user stories from all project managers and business analysts in the sector on the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning in all areas of the organization.

CREDENTIAL.text: Our Chief Information Officer suggested that a horizontal approach would allow efficiency gains in the in-house development or procurement of a solution that caters for the organisation’s needs.
We then got each participant to pen down how artificial intelligence and machine learning could improve each user story, essentially a wishlist.

FINANCIAL.text: Our team of two facilitators alongside the lead project team managers regrouped virtually to decide on the best approach to conduct the virtual design thinking workshop and discussed various tools, methods and platform to collaboratively gather user stories for a group of 30 participants.

A staff would want their claims to be automated through a mobile app by taking snapshots of the parking receipts, a claims processing officer would want the web app to assist with approving whitelisted claims and only highlighting exception cases, and the finance officer would want to only perform an audit only on accounts that breached authorised limits.

MEDICAL.text: After much discussion on the agenda and main objectives of the design thinking workshop, our team of facilitators felt comfortable with selecting the mind map method as the method to gather user stories.

BIOMETRIC.text: According to Wikipedia, a mind map is a diagram used to visually organize information. It is hierarchical and shows relationships among pieces of the whole, created around a single concept, drawn as an image in the center of a blank page.

URL.text: Having participated in a global design thinking workshop, I proposed Miro as the mind map platform as it catered to multi-user collaboration in conjunction with Microsoft Teams as the meeting platform.

IP_ADDRESS.text: I volunteered to design the mind map to fit to the objective of collecting user stories from participants. Centrally, I overlaid the mind map with an image of a neutral network representing the human brain symbolic to artificial intelligence.

NETWORK.text: At the top of the canvas, I placed visuals to remind participants what user stories are, which are personas that we want to gather with use cases for each department across the organisation.

VEHICLE.text: Each branch connected to the central concept referenced a sector in our organisation and its branches referenced specific types of staff in those sectors.

COORDINATES.text: For example, within the administration department, there were three sub-branches representing a staff filing for claims, the claims processing officer, and the finance officer disbursing the funds.
Because participants were asked to empathize with the personas rather than themselves, as a staff in the IT sector, user experiences were captured well in the mind map.

PERSON.text: Design Thinking Reflection – Mohd Amir – May 31, 2020

COMPANY.text: I first used the visualization tool during a Design Sprint on solving a business problem of a start-up rental scooter company.
The scooter company had operational costs higher than revenues, still small user basis and were running out of time on funding.
They have been looking into some business ideas on how to decrease their operational costs through optimization of processes and logistics.

Furthermore, the start-up company considered the idea of generating additional revenues through additional revenue streams from partnering, i.e. users can deliver packages, as well as motivating its existing user base to share ads of the company on social media with the purpose to increase through that the number of existing users.

My goal was to support the start-up company in creating a prototype of how to discover and implement the ideas of a new revenue stream from (i) partnering as well as of (ii) how to increase the user basis.
The suggested solution has to be implemented on their website and/or mobile solution (app).

During the design sprint I drafted a storyboard of how the user will react on advertisement on Facebook or Youtube, click through and go on a landing page, where he can sign-up, customize her/his profile, so that respective to-do's/tasks are displayed for her/him on the main page.
The fulfillment of the tasks and to-do's were will generate credit's for the user which she/he can apply for renting a scooter.

The company otherwise will benefit from fulfillment of the tasks as well – users will share and promote on social media ads from the start-up company leading to increased awareness of the company and hopefully user basis; users will also be able to deliver packages in selected nearby locations in case a scooter is close to their location and the delivery location is in a proximity to their current location.
The visualization tool was instrumental in gathering a useful user feedback and developing the product with relatively small initial time and money effort.
To support the design of the above mentioned solutions I created a storyboard which I visualized using first pen and paper creating a low fidelity prototype.
Then using PowerPoint as well as other software packages I created a medium fidelity prototype.
In creating the visualization, I followed the below described steps:
1) Created a rough storyboard using notes (Post-it's) and markers (Sharpies) to put on paper and described what the user journey will be.
2) When I was finished with the rough storyboard I created a low fidelity prototype with pen and paper.
3) After reviewing and collecting the low fidelity prototype I created a medium fidelity prototype
Using a visualization was an enlightening experience for me.
The need to visualize helped me foster my thinking in more holistic way, e.g. taking the perspective of the user: how he will proceed, what the user might want and/or miss.
It helped me put myself in the situation of the user and not only consider the business perspective (company perspective).

Furthermore, the visualization helped put the story in real context and think of how the product should really look like from a product design perspective, e.g. what kind of colors, images, text and their positioning on the webpage/app should be used.
It helped me collect a useful feedback from potential users before putting a real effort and money in creating an existing and functioning product.
This approach saved time and money and was very effective in confirming/rejecting the hypothesis I created when envisioning how a potential user will deploy the app.
Based on the low fidelity visualization I created the medium fidelity visualization which added an additional layer of complexity, but required still a low effort in terms of time and money.
This medium fidelity visualization was also very useful as it enabled users to see a product with colors, real pictures and even some click-functionalities.

DATE_TIME.text: Challenge: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.
The key insight that I think the Mind Mapping tool helped bring to the foreground was around the need for colleague empathy during any restructure process.
I think the Mind Map was the right tool to choose given the breadth of elements that could impact a reorganisation of this magnitude.

Otherwise, if there are too many inputs there will simply be too much ‘noise’ and my role would shift from thinking creatively about the problem to simply managing the process of data capture and collation.

EMAIL.text: Selection: In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected (e.g., what it is and why)

Initially I had been very concerned with the functional success of the restructure – i.e. did it achieve an optimal technical design, could it be implemented quickly and efficiently, did it remove inefficiency and duplication? Etc.

The only small thing I would do differently to make the process more efficient next time would be to write all the sub-points on post-it notes initially and then start to group them on the map (rather than writing things directly onto the map, which then needed to be rubbed out and changed, etc.)

PHONE.text: I chose to try and apply the Mind Mapping tool to this exercise.

However, through a more expansive brainstorming approach using the mind map I found myself giving more consideration to how colleagues would feel and be impacted by the process (many have been with the company a long time; may have been stuck doing just one thing during that time; some may be eager for change; others apprehensive of it).

Also, I think it would definitely be good to seek a broader range of views and opinions (i.e. getting a small group of colleagues to co-create a mind-map together), as this would be a good way to validate thinking in real-time and minimise the chance of any blind-spots being missed.

ADDRESS.text: I chose this because I thought it could be a good way of capturing all the different dimensions, and elements that impact such a wide and diverse group of individuals.

COMPANY.text: I also wanted to try this tool as it is not one I have used extensively and was therefore one I wanted to practice.

This opened up a whole new line of thinking around colleague engagement both as inputs into the organisational design process as well as in how to communicate the outcomes effectively and secure the maximum buy-in to the new approach.

The caveat to this is that this would need to be kept to a manageable number of colleagues (i.e. 6 to 8 key people like a focus group) in order to be able to manage the process effectively and still be able to input fully yourself.

FINANCIAL.text: It allowed me to brainstorm and get down on paper all the various different facets of the challenge (be they big or small) and then start to cluster and organise these thematically (e.g. training, location, business grade, promotion prospects, etc.)

MEDICAL.text: My initial version was very messy, but with some polish, I think this could also be turned into a good communication tool to help illustrate my thought process and business recommendations in a more interactive and compelling way than a more traditional PowerPoint slide deck.

NETWORK.text: I began with a very large piece of A4 paper and lots of sketching of boxes of ideas, issues, and data points in pencil (as I knew I would be doing a lot of rubbing out and re-writing as the thought process developed)

Towards the latter stages, I spent time trimming down and refining the map a little. I didn’t draw it all out neatly again, but someone could potentially do this, instead I just highlighted the key points that I felt were most important to focus on in the short, medium and long term, as a form of prioritisation (to help avoid a long laundry list of to dos that might never be achieved).

BIOMETRIC.text: After this initial brainstorming process, key themes started to emerge (e.g. technical skills – i.e. SQL database coding, Tableau data visualisation, PowerPoint report writing skills, etc.)

COORDINATES.text: I took these macro themes and placed them on post-it notes, then I was able to interconnect these themes with lines, as well as group individual sub-themes and data points beneath each of them.
I was happy with the outcome and would definitely consider using this tool again in future.

VEHICLE.text: It was definitely a messy and iterative process to begin with, but I was comfortable with this having seen the example in the online video, and the freedom to sketch and make mistakes in this way helped capture a more expansive set of thinking and hopefully reach a more complete final map.

Unlike other reflections you may be privileged to review, this one will be different as I have never purposefully implemented DT nor storytelling as part of my process in the past
I shall not be sharing an anecdote of past presentations and what I have learned from them
Traditional thinking is no longer working for this LOB; therefore, I chose the Design Thinking for Innovation course for a reason
Status quo is no longer acceptable and must learn and adapt to succeed
In the week 2 video "Storytelling Tool", Pedro Sanchez stated "Every great brand with longevity in the retail space……has a story"
it now falls on my shoulders to uncover the story of this LOB to elevate the awareness of the brand

What I have been able to take from the lessons of Design Thinking for Innovation, is that storytelling for business requires the storyteller be able to convey a logical message by understanding the following:
1. Who is my audience (what do they know about the value of this LOB and what is missing from their current understanding – what do they need i.e./ data)?
2. When is the optimal time to tell this story (are they in the frame of mind to retain such information?)
3. Can I communicate a clear sequence of events (does the story have an impactful beginning and does it flow easily and compellingly to the end)?
Can I present an intelligent argument for further investment in this LOB using data from "What is" research?
4. This LOB represents the most emotional connection to our organization, can I describe this in a way to elicit an emotional response from our executive team?
5. Do I allow for moments of reflection (I need to build in unanswered questions that will engage the audience to be intrigued enough to look for answers?)
6. Am I prepared to present solutions or ideas to spark solutions so that no question remains unanswered?

Upon completion of Design Thinking for Innovation, I do feel that I have the tools to more successfully convey the message that our access to data (thanks to our Membership base) is unparalleled but lacks the humanity/empathy that ethnography can provide

As the first part of my approach to overcoming my previously mentioned challenge, DT has reinforced my belief in that such data will contribute to driving transformation and essential to understanding the human connection to this LOB
Secondly, I have come to understand throughout this program that a good story must be relevant and true
Simple and complete. This is what I have been missing in the past.
Upon reflection within this reflection I have been able to pinpoint the fact that I have been providing my audience only with the "wow" information

listing the benefits of the LOB, but not supporting with data, context nor opportunities for the human connection and given no time for digestion of what this LOB truly has to offer to the organization as a whole.
