PHONE.text: THE CHALLLENGE: Describe your challenge, including all relevant information.

My challenge is based around a real life business scenario; this company has a charity health  system managed through a physical contact centre. The key focus of this contact centre is to  receive calls from poor communities on medical issues they face day to day. These contact  centres are managed and run by real medical practitioners. They receive these calls and support  callers with simple advisory on possible actions for recovery through recommendations and  referrals to medical centres close to caller’s location.

The budget for running this centre has been increasing year on year and management is seeking  a cost effective and technology based options to keep the centre still running and at the same  time extent operations to new user groups. I am working with a team both internally and  externally to fix the current problem statement to find an innovative model to deliver a more  cost effective and smart solution adoptable by today’s people.
In your own words, briefly describe the tool you selected (e.g., what it is and  why you selected it for your challenge -- including any appropriate video lecture references)

My selection of Learning Launch is simple; it is one design thinking tool that will help the team  test and experiment our hypothesis with real users and as such quickly pick up on our lessons  including failing for fast turn of strategy.
Describe how you applied the tool you selected to your challenge (e.g., what you  did and how the tool was applied effectively or ineffectively)

So the application of the selected tool was very simple; After working and selecting a virtual  platform running on hosted cloud infrastructure the team is in proof of concept stage with the  technology.
Our old way of delivering our health service had told us a story which we believe we can change  with our innovative strategy.

PERSON.text: A Reflection on the Use of Mind Mapping for Health Professions Education

ADDRESS.text: The delivery of healthcare education for nurses, physicians, dentists, physical therapists, social workers, and pharmacists has historically taken a siloed approach.

DATE_TIME.text: This approach is problematic because these individuals are expected to work together in teams to provide quality patient care, yet they are not trained to do so.
The unstructured setup allows individual ideas and thoughts to flow freely.
In the most recent exercise using the mind mapping technique
After the 20 minutes, each group reviewed their sticky notes and if necessary moved them around for better concept grouping.
The session I described above took place over a total of 4 hours.
This process is amazing for generating a lot of ideas in a very short time.
A lot of very good, actionable ideas were generated and are available for continued discussion and thinking about this wicked problem.
There are other design-thinking tools that could have been used in this exercise.

PHONE.text: To address the “wicked” problem of how might we increase interprofessional educational opportunities across healthcare disciplines
The organizers selected a mind mapping exercise using sticky notes to get participants thinking creatively about how we as educators might address the wicked problem.
Similar concepts are grouped together, allowing ideas to jump around among topics, rather than forcing them down a list.
We gathered together in one room 30 health professions educators and divided them into groups of six.
We had only one rule which was that every idea offered up must in some way be “actionable.”
Each team was challenged to develop at least 50 different ideas over 20 minutes.
As you might expect, the exercise created a lot of noise and excitement in the room as participants brainstormed and wrote down their ideas.
Participants were paired with a participant from another group.
Most of my previous experience with mind mapping exercises has been limited to 90-minute workshops
Each group generated at least 30 ideas, and several groups generated more than 50 ideas.
One downside was the small size of the room in which the activity took place.
In the future, however, I would want to make sure the room setup was appropriate for the size of the group and that the surroundings encouraged creativity.
It rapidly engaged people and moved them outside their comfort zone.
With that said
This method can really create a sense of urgency and move people to action quickly.
In this workshop
This kind of story motivates, helps communicate the problem, and opens the door to envisioning a different future.

EMAIL.text: A national organization convened a group of healthcare educators to participate in a design-thinking workshop.
As we learned in this course, mind mapping is a visual method for helping others to understand how ideas relate to each other and is one of the most universal ways to brainstorm.
I have personally used this technique in multiple workshops and sessions to address difficult and challenging issues in medical education.

Everyone was given a pen and a set of sticky notes and sent to their respective groups to begin brainstorming how we might increase interprofessional educational opportunities across multiple healthcare disciplines.
Each group was assigned a staff person to manage the sticky notes, to group them on a wall according to concepts, and to refuse any idea that was not actionable.
Once this activity was completed
Each participant was asked to share the ideas generated from their group session and to select one best idea for prototyping later that afternoon.
I really appreciated having another 2.5 hours to dig a little deeper and experience design-thinking methodology more fully.
We worked in a small, windowless hotel conference room which was not very conducive to creative thinking – although we did not let that stop us!
Mind mapping was a terrific design-thinking tool to use.
I plan to use this methodology more in future workshops.
I am a fan of storytelling, or using narrative, to develop empathy around an issue or challenge.
We know that patient care is improved when educational barriers are removed, and healthcare providers learn to work cooperatively in teams.
The organizers could have used a story, perhaps a patient story which described a poor patient outcome because of healthcare providers not working together as a team.

COMPANY.text: Miriam’s Field Operations organization needs to reduce the number of technicians in trucks that it sends out into the field to assist customers with troubleshooting their television and broadband issues.
It could also give customers a much better experience that does not involve the customer having to wait at home during a four-hour appointment window for a technician’s visit.

EMAIL.text: Customers call into customer care call centers and chat online about their service issues.
Using a mind map could help identify better ways for Miriam to solve its customers’ problems before having to roll a technician/truck.

Given the process nature of Miriam customers calling into a center, workflows being used, then trouble tickets being recorded, and finally dispatching technicians to troubleshoot, the mind map seems like a good approach to help solve its technician/truck roll challenge.
I opted for a scenario about a broadband customer self-install kit.
When that happens, the customer must call into a call center for help and this frequently requires a technician/truck roll to solve the problem.
While there are instructions in the self-install kit, it became clear that many technician/truck rolls are related to issues outside of the equipment in the kit (e.g., modem/router, cables).

I noted potential pain points for the customer along the way, such as potential areas of confusion or instructions that relied heavily on technical “jargon” that were intended for a non-technical audience.
If a non-tech savvy customer was unable to determine an input vs. an output port on their own, the instructions provided would be of no help.
This insight was likely the source of customer confusion and a failed self-install which would lead to a call to the call center and a potential technician/truck roll.
APPROACH

PHONE.text: Those calls are handled but representatives who follow detailed troubleshooting process flows that ultimately generate trouble tickets that in turn dispatch technicians out to a customer’s home to help troubleshoot and solve a customer’s problem.
SELECTION
Having this knowledge will be critical for the next step, the “what if” phase of the design thinking process that helps to identify how to modify the current situation for the better.
When applying the mind map to Miriam’s processes, I found the challenge to be overwhelming and decided that it might be best to focus on a specific type of reason for a technician/truck roll.

This kit is sent out to customers who order internet service, who want to install the equipment themselves. Quite often, something in the process breaks down and the customer is unable to complete the self- install.

In looking at the volume of calls into a call center, related to the customer self-install kit, I used a mind map to draw out the various process steps a customer goes through during the self-install.

I mapped out the entire customer process from call in to the call customer to place the order for a self- install kit, to receipt of it, opening the contents, reviewing the instructions through to install.
The insight I had from mapping out all the steps a customer must go through to do the self-install, was that the information about which port to plug which cable into could be misconstrued.
My mind map showed a clear gap in the installation process. There were just too many options for a customer to use the cables to connect the router.

This exercise also helped me to see why the “what is” phase of design thinking is crucial. It now seems obvious to me that this step demonstrates the problem in a clearer light so potential solutions in the “what if” phase can be addressed.

ADDRESS.text: There is ample cost in operating the call centers and ample cost to roll a truck and a highly skilled technician out to a customer’s home.

DATE_TIME.text: If Miriam could reduce the number of technician/truck rolls by giving customer options to solve the problem themselves or proactively solve a customer’s problem before (s)he must call in for assistance could save Miriam millions of dollars in operating costs.

Hello, and thank you so much for your review.
The DS-team contented the CEO, the CFO and two employees, one designer and one editor, all of them were female.
The person was a female marketing leader of a medium sized company with around 500 employers.
They called her Tina.

PHONE.text: I hate that lady!
In a Workshop I coached a visualization process and participated an extraordinary turnaround.
Last week I was a coach in a three-day-workshop about business model innovation.
I coached a team of 4 designers who worked in a design studio with a focus on branding and marketing in the B2B sector.
Within three workshop days, we went through a process which was close to a real design thinking  process:
At first, we pointed out the DS-challenge regarding their business model.
Secondly, we defined the target group.
Thirdly we developed three questions and interviewed some people about how the marketing  process in their company was actually working, and which problems usually go along with  marketing.
Fourthly, we described the new customer experience and developed an approach for the new  business model.

Before the workshop took place, I thought about the challenge of applying a design thinking tool and  decided the visualization-tool would suit best for the definition of one special member the target  group.
This was the second step of the process.
I gave the DS-team the assignment to think about one member of their typical target group for three  minutes alone and take some notes.
Then they should share their thoughts.
It turned out, that all DS-members had in mind almost the same picture of one special type of person,  who was standing for their typical target group.
Demographical attributes like age, gender, number of  children and income were very similar.
This surprised me because I knew, that the DS-company had  more than this type of customers.
After that, they visualized the person on a flipchart.
The CFO took a pencil and drew the person, referring  to the instructions, the other DS-members told her (see picture 1).
Then we started thinking about problems which would occur in Tina’s daily work and which were the  jobs-to-be-done to make her happy.
We hang up the flipchart and stood side by side to Tina.
Within this  process, the DS-team talked a lot about their frustration and worries concerning Tina.
The biggest  discussion topic was that Tina does not have the insights of strategic marketing knowledge which the  DS-team needs to do a good job.
When the designer said that, her colleagues agreed.
Insights
I tried to handle the situation and asked them to visualize some positive aspects regarding Tina on the  flipchart as well (in picture 1 you see the red handwriting on the flipchart).
But the frustration was  ongoing, and all of the positive aspects had a negative or unsympathetic touch.
It turned out, that they  cannot do a good job for Tina, as a representative of their main target group.
We started thinking about alternatives for their business model because in step one they constated that  they both worked with medium sized and small companies.
Then they visualized two representatives of  the other target groups in small companies (Marcel und Mia, as you see in picture 2).
The DS-team was  much more creative, and they had many ideas within short time how to make Marcel and Mia satisfied  and do a better job.
In the end, the DS-team decided to change their main target group and, in the future, not to focus Tina,  standing for a marketing leader of a medium sized company with around 500 employees.
The team  decided to change their business model and accompany smaller companies in their marketing  processes.

Pivotal for the decision to make that holistic change were their strong emotions and the  frustration coming along with the visualized Tina and the barriers which hindered the DS-team on doing  a great creative marketing process for Tina.
Approach
The continuing non-verbal confrontation with the flipchart-tall visualized Tina was the key for the DS- team to verbalize the problems regarding the work with their main target group.
Looking back, I think about what would have turned out, if I would have had enriched the process with  even more elements of visualization.
There would have been some possibilities to do so.
For example:

If I - in the first place - had given them the assignment to draw a picture of their typical target group and  not just even to take notes, maybe their distinct problem with Tina would have become visible much  earlier.
Also, I could have asked them to visualize the positive aspects regarding Tina on the flipchart,  rather than writing them down.
In addition to that, I really liked the fact that, in the end, we had two versions of Tina:
On the one hand
we had one flipchart-tall visualized Tina with two catchy attributes like her bag and her plait.
One the
hand we had a smaller version of Tina with the same catchy attributes on a post-it to work with and to  place her where ever she was needed within the creative process (as you see in picture 2)

PHONE.text: As I started this Design for Business Innovation course, I was immediately drawn to the messages in the Physics of Innovation lecture.
As I worked through the course I noted key learnings, knowledge, information from each week, and insights that I knew would be useful to unpack later.
I used the xMind tool (see: http://www.johnson.com/categories/wp-content/tagabout.html) – a really good tool I’d had exposure to previously that allows you build up the Mind Map online.
I flagged the areas on the mind map (using ‘flag’ indicators) where there were real insights/findings relative to our situation.
I also flagged areas where it was appropriate to disseminate a supporting visual, or reference detailed supporting information.
Additionally, I flagged key findings by theme, to highlight some recommendations.

Alongside the Mind Map, I created a summary view of the themed findings/insights – with associated questions for introspection that would provide input to a sharing workshop session with leadership to spark conversation into our real ‘What is’ and ultimately uncover more ‘What is’ information.

For the sharing workshop session, I setup the room with visuals including the Mind Map in large printed view, and other key visuals that supported the findings/insights and used the space to disseminate the information, allowing participants to interact with the visuals at key points in the story telling walkthrough, to validate findings, co-create more findings and gain alignment on our ‘What is’.

I designed the session to step through the key themes in the Mind Map – telling the story, imparting learning/knowledge, posing a question and answer, and allowing participants introspect on that question and answer and co-create further – offering up more information to develop the current picture relative to the insights/findings.
The workshop was designed to be interactive as we unpacked the Mind Map insights together.

In terms of insights, it’s amazing to use a technique like Mind Mapping to distil a large volume of information into something palatable that allows insights to emerge, but it’s also an extremely powerful way of learning and staying “in the question” long enough to gain greater understanding.

The visual aspect the Mind Map provided was an impactful way to theme and distil the information and allow participants to interact with the map and the key messages – evidenced by their questions, and further post-it notes on pain points/challenges.

My own question generated from that early lecture in Week 2 – the Physics of Innovation was: Are we set up for success in our Innovation Unit, how do other parts of the organisation see us depending on their mind-set, and how is this impacting us?
This allowed us to completely unpack the insights distilled into the Mind Map additionally complimented by other techniques (discussed in the approach below)
I realised that in the full sense of design thinking I was largely working on my own for this initial stage.

However, I used this approach and the Mind Mapping technique with its resulting insights as the catalyst to bring new knowledge and learning to leadership and springboard into a fuller design thinking ‘What is’ stage.
What I was uncovering through this mechanism sparked the same thoughts in others in the group and allowed learning and a recognition of mis-aligned mind-sets.
Often, we are experiencing symptoms of a problem we don’t yet have the knowledge to recognise or name!
In this case the learning from the Physics of Innovation lecture was the knowledge that was needed alongside the subsequent lectures on having a prepared mind.

As a result of the above, the insights & findings were further co-created by the group and others and this ultimately allowed us to move to a ‘What if’ stage – applying the design thinking process to our approach to innovation in our unit.

We settled on some early recommendations that would inform our What if stage in terms of education, prepared minds, formalising our innovation practices, and clarifying the difference in our work, to that of other parts of the organisation.

There will be more to come on this as we move through the remaining design thinking stages, but the course, and the technique of Mind Mapping has greatly helped in distilling this knowledge and allowed us ‘hold up a mirror’ to our ‘What is’ to recognise and address the challenges we face innovating in a large organisation.

EMAIL.text: As instructional designer (ID), I was approached to support a professor at the university, where I work, to advise him on how to put his negotiation course online.

As an instructional designer, my focus has always been on creating a learner-focused environment so the challenge was to take a complicated course structure and simplify it for students as well as faculty.

I plan to discuss the Learning Launch Design Tool because I had the opportunity to develop a prototype, 7-week course, and test it by offering it to a small group of 14 professionals (from diverse backgrounds, all working full-time) with the same team — faculty, TA, and ID — who would later implement the full 14-week version for full-time graduate students.
As to who, we knew that working professionals often look for training in negotiation so the course would meet their ongoing needs.
The costs to implement the learning launch were minimal as it required staff time that was already allocated to the project and used tools and processes that are part of the university system.

We anticipated giving refunds if this were an issue to maintain good relations. And the timeframe was short and completed a month prior to the start of fall term, allowing us to make changes, where needed, to the prototype.
The course was structured and designed, applying user-experience effective practices.

Along with the automated grading system that was created, a survey was given to the students at the end of the course to gauge their learning experience with questions focused on their experience with the course structure, content, and assignments.

PHONE.text: When he asked for support, he was looking for someone to help him develop video lectures to replicate his in-class presentations.

Another obstacle was how to replicate the weekly interactions that built a strong student community in the classroom with an online setting where students would interact in a relatively isolating environment.

Added to that challenge was the need to create an online structure for a positive student experience to engage with the materials and activities as well as to automate the students' work in such a way that TAs and professor need only to track it and review it leaving a clear documentation trail and making grading easier.

Our key assumption was that an online negotiation course could be successfully implemented by developing an active student community, through relevant activities and course structure based on user-centered design.
The how was implemented through the existing communications and LMS systems.
The only real cost to anticipate would be the program's reputation (not a minor cost).
Application
Did the automation work without being too complicated for the students? Were the students engaged? Did it free up time for the professor and TA?

A secondary goal was to evaluate the efficacy of offering the course in the online environment. Would the students not only remain engaged but would they achieve the course outcomes and skill building?
All assignments were completed using online tools to aggregate responses in a spreadsheet.
Pass/ fail quizzes were built into the LMS so that students could determine if they were absorbing the material.

DATE_TIME.text: I am currently doing projects for the ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY (WWF) in the Philippines that advocates a new concept of Corporate Social Responsibility, but brought down to the level of an individual, and in particular for the youth. We call this Personal Social Responsibility or Personal CSR 3.0 which is anchored on 3 values: Citizenship – where the individual is aware of his or her responsibility in the community, and society

The reason why our Foundation believes in this concept of Personal CSR for the youth is because of the following reasons: 1. The youth in our region (Asia) comprise majority of our population. Therefore they are a force who can contribute a lot of positive impact for socio-economic development (UNFPA, 2014). 2. Young people are always asking themselves – “How do I create meaning in my life?” “How do I make a difference?” Hence they are constantly looking for avenues to discover what they want to do in life, while finding that sweet spot where they use their talents and passions to serve a specific need in the world (Wong, 2012). 3. Because corporations are always looking for innovative ways to contribute to society, it is recommended that they engage more young people in their CSR efforts because the youth have these innovative ideas, and have the passion and ability to execute them (Klein, 2012)

Obviously , Personal CSR is a big concept that can be a challenge for young people to understand. Hence the project I am working on is a Digital Lifestyle Magazine for the Youth in Asia (starting with those in college). It aims to showcase inspiring stories of young people and organizations who are creating positive social and environmental impact, and who embody the values above. It hopes to show role models that young people in Asia can emulate, and later on realize that doing good for society need not be hard. They can start with themselves and in their own community. We also want it to be digital in order to reach as many youth as possible, in this age of social media and connectivity.

My team and I are currently in the brainstorming stage for the pilot issue. The challenge however was to figure out the right “voice”, “personality” and “content” that we must use in our digital magazine, in a way that will be relevant to our target market.

We even had several arguments because they were struggling to understand how the CSR concept (which normally is discussed among the corporate and academic world) can be brought down to level of young people. Hence our team focused on answering the following questions: Who exactly is the young person that we are targeting? What kind of content will resonate with this young person so he/she can be inspired to act and do good for society?

 Who exactly is the young person that we are targeting?  What kind of content will resonate with this young person so he/she can be inspired to act and do good for society?  How do we reach this young person, and all the other youth who fit this profile?

We used the “Storytelling” tool as a starting point to answer the questions above. I agree with Kazi Regan of Mars Inc. who said in the video compiled in Claire Parodi’s course, that storytelling is a great way to connect with the emotions, characters and values of the people we want to serve (Ale, 2016). It is also relevant for the Digital Magazine, because what we are essentially trying to do is to empower young people by telling stories.
a. Storytelling can allow us to create energy, excitement and passion around a cause and advocacy.
This is exactly what we are trying to do – we are advocating a way of life: to live a lifestyle of contributing to the common good in our own way.
b. Storytelling allows us to make strategy accessible.

The concept of this Personal CSR philosophy is actually result of more than a decade of research on the evolution of Corporate Social Responsibility in Asia, particularly in the Philippines. Our founder believes that in order for the social responsibility initiatives to be effective, youth engagement is key.

For more than a year, our Foundation has actually collected real interviews with young people to talk about how they are volunteering to help society (https://www.youtube.com/user/vdrake). I also got to share stories from youth awardees that our Foundation recognized who are exemplars of this Personal CSR advocacy: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y1ZQmZmkaDD, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HePCiQaZo2X,

During the brainstorming we had a week ago, I showed these interviews to our Digital Magazine team. As I mentioned, prior to that, we had several discussions and even arguments about CSR, and what exactly we are trying to achieve.

Some of us in the team are also teachers in a local college, where we teach the subject Social Responsibility and Good Governance. Our experience was that although there are many inspiring stories of young people doing amazing work that tries to address social problems in developing country, many of our students are not aware about these stories.
But exposure is the key to get these young people to be engaged.

The showcasing of real stories to the Digital Magazine team was effective in contextualizing the kind of direction we can take when creating our content. It also helped us put a “face” to the target market.
We also identified cases of social media content from pop culture that trended in our region, which gave us an insight as to the digital strategy to reach the target youth.

This strategy involves creating content that is as “sticky” as the current pop culture trends, but has the messaging that we want to get across. We need to use hashtags to maximize the multimedia platforms, particularly mobile social media, so we can reach more audience.

The main point was that we must focus on these personal stories. We eventually decided to adopt the title of the video blog, and launch “CSR Stories” as a pilot to test this content to our target market.

This storytelling tool gave me the insight that stories are indeed more relevant and more resonating for people. To deconstruct a business and academic concept like CSR, into shareable content in a Digital Lifestyle magazine, seemed pretty daunting for our team.

This makes me realize that stories must be indeed the center of our content. We can show short video clips (like an Instagram or Vine video) of young people sharing their “CSR Stories”. We also realized that there are existing content platforms like “Humans of New York” that have executed this strategy of storytelling well, in a way that became a viral movement across the world.
Therefore, this became one of our benchmarks for the Digital Magazine.

These insights eventually allowed our team to construct this model which represents (for now), the goal that our Digital Magazine must create: Using the social media hashtag #LiveYourCSR, we want to create a movement for young people to go through these stages of being involved (attending events, engaging with our magazine content)  then deciding to volunteer with a purpose (volunteering in an organization of their choice)  then committing to this concept of Personal CSR with Citizenship, Sustainability and Social Responsibility,  then deciding to Make CSR a Lifestyle by signing some sort of Personal Social Responsibility Pledge which we will put in our site.

It may still be a little vague and general at this point, but at least for our team, it was a good step towards concretizing the direction we want to invite our readers to, when they engage with our Digital Magazine.

COMPANY.text: Story telling as a primary tool
I use story telling as a primary tool to help them visualize the  situation they are in and it helps them approach the problem from a different perspective.
Multiple  perspectives lets us break down the problem into simpler blocks and helps understand the inter  linkages and leads to simple solutions.
Story telling always helps the team to participate, empathize  and co-create solutions which also solves change management complexities.
I was in a situation where we were coming up with a new digital user experience strategy for a  client with a large customer base.
The client wanted to develop a strategy for expanding the current  customer base.
Within the client organization multiple entities were involved in the process such as  IT, Business, Branding and marketing.

Each one had different priorities and the design strategy being proposed either had too much complexity to be implemented by the IT team or too simple for  business to justify incremental revenues due to the new strategy or it simply did not meet the  branding requirements.
I used the story telling method where, all stakeholders were brought into a room
this being a great  challenge as the teams were spread across Asia and the US.
However, once the teams were in one  common location, it provided us a platform for resolving differences immediately.
The different user experience elements were handed over to small teams which had a mix of all the stakeholder  teams and User experience experts.
The teams came up with designs and developed their own  stories to tell as to why and how their designs were arrived at.
These stories were relatable by the  rest of the stakeholders as it had business implications which they had faced in their day-today  operations.
The teams were able to discuss and agree upon experience element designs.

What I learnt from this exercise was that even teams which do not see eye-to-eye in normal  business context can be made to understand each other’s perspectives by bringing them together  and making them co-create stories and solutions that solve critical organizational issues.

By  providing an environment to make them co-create solutions and helping them share with the rest  of their team, they were able to see each other’s perspectives and agree upon a middle way so that  they can go ahead for implementation and hence make way for growth of the organization.
Story telling is a tool that I believe that I will use in future as well in situations where I need to make  and push complex decisions for an organization.
It involves all stakeholders to think and deliberate  on each other’s perspective at a one-on-one level in a conducive setting without the interference of  organizational dynamics.
The solution or strategy that comes out of it is the most optimal and not necessarily the right solution.
But it works as all team members have jointly developed it and will  be earnest enough to see through its success.

EMAIL.text: The special kind of  industry and environment did no provide many partners or time for surveys and not much money for  external graphic designers as well as very few industry bench marks.
We aimed to find out what our two different  target groups expected and what met their information needs without spending all budget and  efforts at once.
Starting with one, we changed the website and came back to five chosen main customers to get  qualitative feedback and including their ideas.
In intervals of 2 weeks the  marketing team closely monitored the website movements and visits and analyzed the numbers  compared to previous numbers.
We worked this into the next  round of the internal “Counsel” and adapted some aspects.

Like this, internal as well as external stakeholders had the feeling to be involved and were all happy  with the result, marketing did not struggle with different parties fighting over taste and opinion.
This case made very clear that it takes much  more time (here almost half a year) than expected and many people involved when being visually  and content-wise creative and customer-oriented.
Building a new website could have been done by using mind maps, collecting ideas from everyone  and then internally implementing the ideas.

The Learning Launch tool is  limited in terms of feasibility; you’d need customers who are willing to participate, an extended time  frame and the team needs to be very patient as results only come step by step and are often revised.

PHONE.text: The target group was very  special and narrow and within the company there were many diverse opinions on how the new  website should look like.

Therefore, the marketing team decided to use the Learning Launch tool  incorporating customers and employees in order to design an appropriate website step by step and  including most important stakeholders into the process.
It should not be a shot in the dark, but an experimental and successive learning  process until we had the perfect website.
After building an internal team of 15 people, at least one from each department, we defined the first  three basic changes to be made on the website (being color, menu layout and homepage picture)
Circling some rounds like this, the team agreed on  what should be changed, and the changes were implemented (went live)
Following the first interval, we asked 5 other main customers who  agreed on cooperating in this project, for their opinion and impression.

Next steps of changes (e.g. product  pictures, portfolio structure, “about us” section and many more) were defined and executed as  described above in a 2-week interval until the whole website was restructured and redesigned.

Seeing this being successful, I decided to use the Learning Launch tool for many other challenges,  avoiding spending money and effort in a creative process that could not be driven by just a few  marketing persons, but successively develops by many.
Marketing is full of these challenges, so we need  to be open for opinions and learn how others can help effectively.
Visualization would have helped to give example sites and decide quickly if that was ok or not. But  then it would have been quite limited to what a few people suggested.

In this case the Learning Launch might have been the best choice, but for a frequent actualization of  the website the Visualization tool might be more appropriate as the frame of the website is already  set.

PERSON.text: I am a Third-year engineering student at a renowned university in India.

I have always found out that expressing my ideas and methodologies to my teachers just through vocal communication is very  difficult and many a time this happened that some of my ideas started getting rejected, but a similar  idea from one of my classmates was appreciated.
I started feeling that I lacked speaking skills or maybe  had some issue with interacting with my teachers.
I already had received so  many prizes in debates, literature competitions and was a good orator.
Then I thought why not find out  what was so special in that classmate of mine who was always successful in this.
I understood that more  than the information, efficiently conveying them and to make others easily understand the thing was  the trick!
The lack of creative content in my delivery of the thoughts made me try out the visualization design tool.
I felt that there couldn't be anything more apt than practically implementing this in everyday life.
As I  selected visualization as my design thinking tool slowly and steadily, I started getting the positive results.
I tried making impressive PPTs, some project prototypes, drawings, 3D models, illustrations and much  more to explain my ideas to the class.
It turned out that I was pretty good at making designs.
Slowly I got  a hold on the aesthetics and started excelling in it.
I took 3 days to research  and finally came on a conclusion to do a project on "Hand gesture recognition for the deaf people".
Tp  explain my views, I made an interactive presentation which consisted of hand gesture gifs, and I also  made an infographic to explain the chronology of the SDLC model that I would be using.
My faculty was just astonished to see my exceptional work and she also sent my project for a national  competition which I won later!
From that day onwards I understood that only having innovative ideas is  not enough but to express them in the best way possible.
I learnt that visualization can really make our  concepts crystal clear and is much easier to grasp for others too.
Not just presentations but the basic  geometric designs or even the freehand mappings we draw to explain our things can drastically change  the output of the process.
I will also try incorporating more tools for better innovation and efficiency in  upcoming tasks.
One addition to this could be adding more interesting tools like storytelling to connect with the  audience as well as the users.

This would make a major impact on the deaf people as they would easily  understand whatever my app needed to convey through comic strips or maybe audio to text translator  for some inspirational stories that I might tell all other normal people.

DATE_TIME.text: The project duration is  estimated in 3 months and it includes the training session for all the stakeholders (agents and  providers)

During the first two weeks we organize our first meetings we organize with agents and  providers to try to understand the high level process and depict it into basic workflows to  ensure the activity was clear.
After this sessions we spend 2 weeks to organize tours in the agents and providers offices to  see how is the daily activity and how their interact with the current tools.

Once the activity is clear, we went more in detail and we organize face to face meeting with  the agents and  providers to see how they manage their tasks, how they tackle their problems  and how they feel with the existing tools.
After that we present a journey map that represents their daily activity with the tasks,  problems and priorities in different scenarios to receive their feedback and test our  hypothesis.

The second month is centered in the build of the app and to present to the users wireframes of  the application as well as walkthrough of the navigation to ensure that all the activities, tasks  and suggestions are accomplished.
By applying this methodology both users (agents and providers) understood better their  activity and the benefits of implementing the new tool.
It also provide them a wide vision of  the whole business and understand the problems of the others allowing a more empathic  behaviour between them.

It also provide them a more sense of collaboration and satisfaction  after presenting during the last meetings the prototypes and the final solution to the rest of  the stakeholders and they started to think on how they can improve it.

Next time I would like to improve the organization of the interviews (with online solutions) to  increase the exploration involve more people in the co creation of solution that is key to  transform the activities and the organizations.

AGE.text: customer meeting trying to understand a process in greater detail
These could be logs, audit traces, print outs, anything
Then I try to piece the flow of events one after another in chronological event of say time
When I feel I have a hunch of where the root cause is or  whenever I am completely stuck in my analytical track, I resort to visualizing the journey of events
As a process, I always deliberately, set the key statement aside, temporarily
Then I start drawing the facts ‘what I know’ say in boxes

Engaging in this process, has multiple benefits, almost immediately I can see if  I have made false assumptions, or reveals that I need to look for more data, or it simply solidifies the  inferences drawn

Another benefit of this visualization practical is that almost immediately I can see if the processes /events  are indeed working as designed (not a defect) else these actions serve are valuable aids to recreate the  issue
Visualizing issues and documenting them also helps the testing teams down line who can now  inspect these visuals and prepare their test cases accordingly
When meeting clients,  using props like post-it notes, charts etc., serve as great aids in understanding the requirements, both  expressed and unexpressed
Many a times, I have used these visual tools to map solutions to  requirements, thus saving a lot of time and effort
Functional diagrams, flow charts, Visio mind maps, are  all tools I have used both understand and explain complex concepts
On many instances, the group or  individual can see errors or missing pieces and quickly correct course when explaining requirements to  us
Another benefit of using a multi nodal visual approach, is that the core verbal discussions become  healthier and productive
These visual aids then  spur the process of demystifying the requirements
Many a times, these aids help me recollect vital points  and fill the gaps in our recollection
Using white boards, flow charts to represent process flows, design diagrams allow me to  understand the technical challenges in a much better form
